{{smaller block|<poem>Thy creatures ''wrong'' thee, O thou sov’reign Good!
Thou art not loved because not understood.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Happy Solitude—Unhappy Men (trans.).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy friendship thus thy judgment ''wronging''
With praises not to me belonging.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iii., Int.}}}}

'''wrong-doer''' (rông′dö″ėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who does wrong, or commits wrongful or reprehensible acts; any offender against the moral law.
{{smaller block|Especially when we see the ''wrong-doer'' prosperous do we feel as if the injustice of fortune ought to be redressed.
{{right|''Channing'', Perfect Life, p. 10.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''law'', one who commits a tort or trespass; a tort-feaser.

'''wrong-doing''' (rông′dö″ing), ''n.'' The doing of wrong; behavior the opposite of what is right; blameworthy action in general.

'''wronge†''', '''wrongen†'''. Middle English forms of ''wrung''.

'''wrongeous†''', ''a.'' An old spelling of ''wrongous''.

'''wronger''' (rông′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''wrong'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who inflicts wrong or harm; an injurer; a misuser.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hold, shepherd, hold! learn not to be a ''wronger''
Of your word. ''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 3.</poem>
Caitiffs and ''wrongers'' of the world. ''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}

'''wrongful''' (rông′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ME. ''wrongful;'' < ''wrong'', ''n.'', + ''-ful.''] Full of or characterized by wrong; injurious; unjust; unfair: as, a ''wrongful'' taking of property.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''wronghearted''' (rông′här″ted), ''a.'' Wrong in heart or sensibility; not right or just in feeling.

'''wrongheartedness''' (rông′här″ted-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being wronghearted; perversity of feeling.
{{smaller block|Wrong-headedness may be as fatal now as ''wrong-heartedness.''
{{right|''The Century,'' XXIX. 910.}}}}

'''wrongless''' (rông′les), ''a.'' [< ''wrong, n.,'' + ''-less.''] Void of wrong. [Rare.]

'''wronglessly''' (rông′les-li), ''adv.'' Without wrong or harm; harmlessly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He was . . . honourably courteous, and ''wronglessly'' valiant.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney,'' Arcadia, i.}}}}

'''wrongly''' (rông′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''wrongliche;'' < ''wrong'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a wrong or erroneous manner; unjustly; mistakenly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou . . . wouldst not play false,
And yet wouldst ''wrongly'' win.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.,'' Macbeth, i. 5. 23.}}}}

'''wrongminded''' (rông′mīn″ded), ''a.'' Having a mind wrongly inclined; entertaining erroneous or distorted views.

'''wrongness''' (rông′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wrongnesse;'' < ''wrong, a.,'' + ''-ness.''] '''1†.''' Crookedness; wryness; unevenness. ''Prompt. Parv.,'' p. 534.—'''2.''' The state or condition of being wrong or erroneous; heinousness; faultiness.
{{smaller block|The best have great ''wrongnesses'' within themselves, which they complain of, and endeavour to amend.
{{right|''Butler,'' Analogy of Religion. (''Latham.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''wrongness'' of murder is known by a moral intuition.
{{right|''H. Spencer,'' Data of Ethics, § 14.}}}}

'''wrongous''' (rông′us), ''a.'' [Also ''wrongeous;'' < ME. ''wrongous'', for earlier ''wrongwis'', ''wrangwis'' (= Sw. ''vrångvis''), wrong, iniquitous; < ''wrong'' + ''wise''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''righteous.''] '''1†.''' Wrongful; unjust; improper.
{{smaller block|<poem>I will not father my bairn on you,
Nor on no ''wrongous'' man.</poem>
{{right|''Childe Vyet'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 77).}}}}
'''2.''' In ''Scots law'', not right; unjust; illegal: as, ''wrongous'' imprisonment.
{{smaller block|Every wrong must be judged by the first violent and ''wrongous'' ground whereupon it proceeds.
{{right|''James I.'', To Bacon, Aug. 25, 1617.}}}}

'''wrongously†''' (rông′us-li), ''adv.'' [Also ''wrongeously;'' < ME. ''wrongously;'' < ''wrongous'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] Unjustly; wrongfully; unfairly.
{{smaller block|<poem>Here haue we done and shewid curtessy,
Where to ''wrongously'' uillanous ye doo,
To thys noble damicel and lady.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1857.}}}}

'''Wronski’s theorem.''' See ''theorem.''

'''wroot†''', ''v.'' An old spelling of ''root''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wrot†.''' An old spelling of ''wrote''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wrote<sup>1</sup>''' (rōt). Preterit and obsolete or vulgar past participle of ''write.''

'''wrote<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''root''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wroth''' (rôth), ''a.'' [< ME. ''wroth'', ''wrooth'', < AS. ''wrāth'', angry (= OS. ''wrēth'' = D. ''wreed'', cruel, = Icel. ''reithr'' = Sw. Dan. ''vred'', angry); prob. orig. ‘twisted,’ perverse (= MHG. ''reit'', ''reid'', curled, twisted), < ''wrīthan'', pret. ''wrath'', twist, writhe: see ''writhe.'' Hence ult. ''wrath'', ''n.''] Ex-

readings.c3s1:
¶
'''wrought-iron''' (rât′ī″ėrn), ''n.'' Iron that is or may be wrought into form by forging or rolling, and that is capable of being welded; malleable iron. See ''iron.''

'''wrung''' (rung). Preterit and past participle of ''wring.''

'''wry<sup>1</sup>''' (rī), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wried'', ppr. ''wrying.'' [< ME. ''wrien'', ''wryen'', < AS. ''wrigian'', drive, tend, turn, bend. Cf. ''wrick'', ''wrig'', ''wriggle.'' Hence ''wry''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'', ''awry.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To turn; bend; wind; twist or twine about, with or without change of place.
{{smaller block|How well a certain ''wrying'' I had of my neck became me.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, ii.}}
The first with divers crooks and turnings ''wries.''
{{right|''P. Fletcher'', Purple Island, v.}}}}
'''2.''' To swerve or go obliquely; go awry or astray; deviate from the right course, physically or morally.
{{smaller block|<poem>And she sproong as a colt doth in the trave,
And with her heed she ''wryed'' faste awey.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 97.}}
<poem>No manere mede shulde make him ''wrye'',
ffor to trien a trouthe be-twynne two sidis.</poem>
{{right|''Richard the Redeless'', ii. 84.}}
<poem>How many
. . . murder wives much better than themselves
For ''wrying'' but a little!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 1. 5.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To turn; twist aside.
{{smaller block|<poem>Soone thei can ther hedys a-way ''wrye'',
And to faire speche lightly ther erys close.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 63.}}}}

'''wrong''' (rông), ''adv.''   [< ''wrong, a.'']   In a wrong manner; not rightly; erroneously; incorrectly; amiss; ill.
{{smaller block|The right divine of kings to govern ''wrong.''
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, iv. 188.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To go wrong.''' See ''go.''}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Your strong possession much more than your right,
Or else it must ''go wrong'' with you and me.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 41.}}}}

'''wrong''' (rông), ''v. t.''   [< ''wrong, n.'']   '''1.''' To do wrong to; treat unfairly, unjustly, or harmfully; do or say something injurious or offensive to; injure; harm; oppress; offend.
{{smaller block|You ''wrong'' me, sir, thus still to haunt my house.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 4. 73.}}}}
'''2.''' To be the cause of wrong or harm to; affect injuriously; be hurtful to; in an old nautical use, to take the wind from the sails of, as a ship in line with another to windward.
{{smaller block|All authoritie being dissolved, want of government did more ''wrong'' their proceedings than all other crosses whatsoever. Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 267.

It [a play] is good, though ''wronged'' by my over great expectations, as all things else are. ''Pepys'', Diary, I. 149.

To use the seaman’s phrase, we were very much ''wronged'' by the ship that had us in chase.
{{right|''Smollett'', Roderick Random, lxv.}}}}
'''3.''' To be in the wrong in regard to; view or consider wrongly; give an erroneous seeming to; put in the wrong, or in a false light. {{smaller block|<poem>Thy creatures ''wrong'' thee, O thou sov’reign Good!
Thou art not loved because not understood.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Happy Solitude—Unhappy Men (trans.).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thy friendship thus thy judgment ''wronging''
With praises not to me belonging.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, iii., Int.}}}}

'''wrongfully''' (rông′fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a wrong manner; in a manner contrary to the moral law or to justice; unjustly: as, to accuse one ''wrongfully;'' to suffer ''wrongfully.''

'''wrongfulness''' (rông′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being wrong or wrongful; injustice.

'''wronghead''' (rông′hed), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''wrong'' + ''head.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Same as ''wrongheaded.'' [Rare.]

'''II.''' ''n.'' A wrongheaded person. [Rare.]

'''wrongheaded''' (rông′hed″ed), ''a.''   [< ''wronghead'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Characterized by or due to perversity of the judgment; obstinately opinionated; misguided; stubborn.
{{smaller block|A ''wrongheaded'' distrust of England.

'''wrongheadedly''' (rông′hed″ed-li), ''adv.'' In a wrongheaded manner; obstinately; perversely.
{{smaller block|He [Johnson] . . . then rose to be under the care of Mr. Hunter, the head-master, who, according to his account, was very severe, and ''wrongheadedly'' severe.

{{smaller block|Using their ''wryed'' countenances, instead of a vice, to turn the good aspects of all that shall sit near them.

<poem>Guests by hundreds — not one caring

'''3.''' Figuratively, to pervert; alter.

{{smaller block|They have wrested and ''wryed'' his [Christ’s] doctrine, and like a rule of lead have applied it to men’s manners.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i.}}}}

<poem>Ill slant eyes interpret the straight sun,
But in their scope its white is ''wried'' to black.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Swinburne'', At Eleusis.}}}}

'''wry'''<sup>1</sup> (rī), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''wry''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' Cf. ''awry.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Abnormally bent or turned to one side; in a state of contortion; twisted; distorted; askew.

<poem>With fair black eyes and hair and a ''wry'' nose.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', tr. of Horace’s Art of Poetry.}}}}

{{smaller block|He calls them [the clergy] the Saints with Screw’d Faces and ''wry'' Mouths.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 232.}}}}

{{smaller block|He ’s one I would not have a ''wry'' thought darted against, willingly. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, ii. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|Every ''wry'' step by which he imagines himself to have declined from the path of duty affrights him when he reflects on it. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, II. xv.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To make a wry face''' or '''mouth,''' to manifest disgust, displeasure, pain, or the like, by distorting or puckering up the face or mouth.}}

{{smaller block|You seem resolved to do credit to our mystery, and die like a man, without ''making wry mouths.''
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, xxxiv.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A twisting about, or out of shape or course; distortion; a distorting effect. [Rare or prov. Eng.]

'''wry<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''wryen'', ''wrien'', ''wreon'', < AS. ''wreón'', *''wrīhan'', ONorth. ''wrīa'' (pp. ''wrigen''), cover, clothe. Cf. ''rig''<sup>2</sup>.]   To cover; clothe; cover up; cloak; hide.

'''wrybill''' (rī′bil), ''n.'' A kind of plover, ''Anarhynchus frontalis'', of New Zealand, having the bill bent sidewise. See second cut under ''plover''.

'''wry-billed''' (rī′bild), ''a.'' Having the bill awry or bent sidewise: as, the ''wry-billed'' plover. See second cut under ''plover''.

'''wryly''' (rī′li), ''adv.''   [< ''wry''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In a wry, distorted, or awkward manner.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
